title: Re-evaluation of pectin (E 440i) and amidated pectin (E 440ii) as food additives
authors: EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food (ANS), Mortensen A, Aguilar F, Crebelli R, Di Domenico A, Dusemund B, et al.
funder: European Food Safety Authority; requestor: European Commission; question numbers EFSA-Q-2011-00528 and EFSA-Q-2011-00758; adopted 17 May 2017.
result: Pectin (E 440i) consists mainly of the partial methyl esters of polygalacturonic acid and their ammonium, sodium, potassium and calcium salts, extracted in aqueous medium from edible plant material, citrus peels and apple pomace being the main sources; amidated pectin (E 440ii) also contains amides, produced by treatment with ammonia, with not more than 25% of total carboxyl groups amidated. The backbone is 1,4-linked alpha-D-galacturonic acid intercalated by 2-linked L-rhamnosyl residues, with side chains mainly of galactose and arabinose. High-methoxyl pectins (more than 50% methylated) gel below about pH 3.6 with a cosolute, typically sucrose, above 55% by weight; low-methoxyl pectins gel with calcium ions. Authorised in the EU as Group I additives at quantum satis in almost all categories, not in infant formulae (13.1.1), and at 10,000 mg/kg in foods for special medical purposes for infants and young children (13.1.5.1, 13.1.5.2); jams are among the quantum satis uses, and consumers also add pectins to thicken jams. Main contributors to refined exposure: flavoured fermented milk products, flavoured drinks, processed fruit and vegetables and desserts. In 7 healthy men, 88.4% (SD 10.5%) of a 5 g dose was recovered in the terminal ileum (Saito et al., 2005); healthy volunteers excreted 3.5% (women) and 4.8% (men) of dietary pectin in faeces, ileostomy patients 85% (women) and 53% (men) (Holloway et al., 1983). Pectins are not absorbed intact but extensively fermented by intestinal microbiota; the main end products are acetic, propionic and butyric acids, absorbed from the colon; methyl ester groups are cleaved in ileostomy and colostomy fluids with release of methanol (Knaup et al., 2008). Human studies: serum cholesterol fell about 8% with 12 g/day for 3 weeks in 12 healthy men (Durrington et al., 1976) and about 5% with 15 g/day in middle-aged men (Keys et al., 1961); 36 g/day (515 mg/kg bw per day) for 6 weeks in 5 healthy men was associated with abdominal distension and increased flatus in some individuals, judged undesirable but not adverse (Cummings et al., 1979). Refined brand-loyal exposure at the 95th percentile reached 442.0 mg/kg bw per day in toddlers. The Panel concluded that there is no need for a numerical ADI and no safety concern for the general population at the reported uses; data did not allow assessment of the 1% use level in foods for special medical purposes for infants and young children. Chronic, reproductive and developmental rat studies reported to the International Pectin Producers Association by Industrial Bio-Test Laboratories lacked a control group and were judged inadequate.
